verdict.rationale: Across the cited texts God or the Spirit is the grammatical agent of the perception and teaching verbs, and the believer is the recipient. In 1 Corinthians 2:10 God revealed (apekalypsen, a completed past action in the active voice) these things through the Spirit, who searches (eraunai, ongoing simple statement of fact) the deep things of God. In verse 12 we received the Spirit so that we may know (eidomen). In verse 13 the words are Spirit-taught (didaktois pneumatos, meaning taught by the Spirit). In verse 14 the natural person is not able to know (ou dynatai gnonai) because such things are spiritually examined (anakrinetai, an ongoing simple statement of fact in the passive voice, meaning the action is done to them). John 16:13 has the Spirit guide (hodegesei, a future action) into all the truth. Ephesians 1:18 has the eyes of the heart enlightened (pephotismenous, a completed action whose result still stands, in the passive voice). Luke 24:45 has Christ open (dianoixen) the mind to understand the Scriptures. Psalm 119:18 petitions God to open (gal, from the Hebrew verb galah meaning uncover) the eyes to see wonders in the torah (the law of Moses). The pattern spans law and writings, prophecy, gospel, and epistle. The genuine open question the words leave is scope, whether this illumination adds new content or grants understanding of the already given word, and whether the all in all the truth is exhaustive or apostolic, but no reading reverses the core claim that the Spirit gives believers spiritual understanding of God's word.

scripture.force: God revealed (apekalypsen, a completed past action in the active voice, third person singular) these things to us through the Spirit (dia tou pneumatos, meaning through the Spirit), and the Spirit searches (eraunai, ongoing simple statement of fact in the active voice, third person singular) all things, even the deep things (ta bathe, the deep things) of God. The word-form analysis fixes God as the subject who reveals and the Spirit as the searching agent, with believers as recipients in the dative case (the 'to-X' grammatical form) hemin (meaning to us). Revelatory and investigative action is bound to the divine Spirit.

As no one knows (egnoken, a completed action whose result still stands, third person singular) the things of a man except the man's own spirit, so no one has known (egnoken, same form, a completed action whose result still stands) the things of God except the Spirit of God. The analogy grounds the claim that only the divine Spirit possesses inside knowledge of God, which is why Spirit-given access is required for others to know.

We received (elabomen, a completed past action) the Spirit who is from God (to ek tou theou, meaning the one from God), expressed in a purpose clause hina eidomen (meaning so that we may know, in the subjunctive mood, first person plural) so that we may know the things freely given (charisthenta, meaning graciously given) to us by God. Knowing the gifted truths of God is grammatically conditioned on receiving the divine Spirit.

We speak these things not in words taught by human wisdom (didaktois anthropines sophias, meaning taught by human wisdom) but in words taught by the Spirit (didaktois pneumatos, meaning taught by the Spirit), interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people (pneumatikois pneumatika synkrinontes, meaning matching spiritual things with spiritual people). The verbal adjective taught (didaktos) with the from-form Spirit (genitive pneumatos, the 'from-X' grammatical form) makes the Spirit the explicit source of the instruction. The word taught (didaktos) is a near hapax (a word that occurs only once or rarely in the entire Bible), three tokens in two verses, but the parallel taught by human wisdom (didaktois anthropines sophias) inside the same clause disambiguates its sense by direct antithesis.

The natural person (psychikos anthropos, meaning the unspiritual or soul-driven person) does not receive (ou dechetai, ongoing simple statement of fact in the middle/passive voice, third person singular) the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he is not able to know them (ou dynatai gnonai, meaning is not able to know, in the infinitive form). Because they are spiritually examined (pneumatikos anakrinetai, meaning are spiritually discerned, in the ongoing passive form, third person singular). The ongoing passive form of examine (anakrino) plus the modal not-able (ou dynatai) grammatically forecloses the natural faculty and makes Spirit-given discernment the necessary condition for apprehending God's word.

Who has known (egno, a completed past action) the mind of the Lord (noun kyriou, meaning the mind of the Lord) so as to instruct him, but we have the mind of Christ (noun Christou echomen, meaning we have the mind of Christ, ongoing simple statement of fact, first person plural). The argument closes by giving believers the mind of Christ (noun Christou), the cognitive faculty that the natural person of verse 14 lacked, completing the contrast.

The anointing (chrisma, meaning anointing) which you received from him remains (menei, meaning remains or abides) in you, and you have no need that anyone teach you (ou chreian echete hina tis didaske hymas, in the present subjunctive mood, naming an ongoing possible action), but as his anointing teaches you (didaskei hymas, ongoing simple statement of fact, third person singular) concerning all things and is true and is not a lie. The word anointing (chrisma) occurs only here and in verse 20, a hapax cluster (a cluster of words that occur only once in the entire Bible) confined to 1 John, but teach (didasko) in the simple present-tense statement names the teaching action plainly. The clause about needing no human teacher reads in context against the deceivers of verses 18 to 26.

When the Spirit of truth (to pneuma tes aletheias, meaning the Spirit of the truth) comes, he will guide you (hodegesei hymas, a future action in the active voice, third person singular) into all the truth (eis ten aletheian pasan, meaning into all the truth), for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce (anangelei, a future action in the active voice, third person singular) to you the things that are coming (ta erchomena, meaning the things coming). The verb guide (hodegeo) elsewhere is literal leading of the blind (Matthew 15:14, Luke 6:39), so the sense here is metaphorical leading into comprehension. The future tense and the second person plural leave open whether all the truth is exhaustive or bounded to the apostolic circle being addressed.

The Helper or Advocate (ho parakletos, meaning the one called alongside, the Helper), the Holy Spirit whom the Father will send in my name, that one will teach you all things (didaxei hymas panta, a future action in the active voice, third person singular) and will remind you (hypomnesei, meaning will bring back to remembrance) of all that I said to you. The Spirit's teaching office toward the disciples is explicit, paired with reminding of already spoken words.

Paul prays that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ may give (doe, in the optative mood, expressing a wish or prayer) to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation (pneuma sophias kai apokalypseos, meaning a spirit of wisdom and unveiling) in the knowledge (en epignosei, meaning in deep knowledge) of him. The wisdom and revelatory faculty for knowing God is requested as a gift, with the words for spirit (pneuma), wisdom (sophia), and revelation (apokalypsis) clustered, echoing the Hebrew Spirit of wisdom (ruach chokmah, meaning Spirit of wisdom) of Isaiah 11:2.

The eyes of your heart having been enlightened (pephotismenous, a completed action whose result still stands, in the passive participle form, accusative plural masculine) for you to know (eis to eidenai, meaning so as to know, in the perfect-tense infinitive) what is the hope of his calling and the riches of his inheritance. The perfect passive form of enlighten (photizo) names a completed illumination wrought upon the believer, and the purpose is comprehension of what is already declared. The object here is understanding of given content, not new content.

Then he opened (dienoixen, a completed past action in the active voice, third person singular) their mind (ton noun, meaning the mind) so as to understand the Scriptures (tou synienai tas graphas, meaning so as to understand the writings). Here the object of the opening is explicitly the written Scriptures (graphas, meaning written documents), and the agent is Christ acting on the disciples' mind (noun). This is the clearest text tying divinely given understanding directly to comprehension of the existing word.

Open (gal, the command form of the Hebrew verb galah, meaning uncover or unveil) my eyes (enay, meaning my eyes) that I may behold (we-abbitah, from the Hebrew verb nabat meaning to look intently) wonders (niphlaot, meaning wonderful things) out of your law (mi-toratecha, meaning from your torah or instruction). The psalmist petitions God to open his eyes for perception of wonders that are already in the written torah (the law of Moses). The agent of opening is God, the recipient is the worshiper, and the object of sight is the existing word, a direct Old Testament prototype of the illumination pattern.

The Spirit of the LORD (ruach YHWH, meaning Spirit of Yahweh) will rest on him, a Spirit of wisdom and understanding (ruach chokmah u-binah, meaning Spirit of wisdom and understanding), of counsel and might, of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. The fourfold spirit (ruach) plus cognitive nouns wisdom (chokmah), understanding (binah), and knowledge (daat) is the Old Testament pattern that links the Spirit to wisdom and understanding, the same cluster Ephesians 1:17 echoes with spirit of wisdom (pneuma sophias).

complicating_texts.resolution: The clause you have no need that anyone teach you (ou chreian echete hina tis didaske hymas) could be read to abolish ordinary instruction and so over-prove the case into anti-teaching. The present subjunctive mood (ongoing possible action) and the immediate context resolve it. John writes this against the deceivers, the antichrists (antichristoi) of verses 18 to 26, so the contrast is the Spirit's protective discernment versus seducers, not the Spirit versus all teachers. The anointing's (chrisma) didactic role is the safeguarding knowledge the Spirit gives, which is consistent with the broader illumination pattern, not against it.

The phrase he will guide you into all the truth (hodegesei hymas eis ten aletheian pasan) with the future tense and second person plural is spoken to the upper-room circle, raising whether guide into all the truth extends to ordinary believers or is a bounded apostolic promise, especially given he will announce the things coming (anangelei ta erchomena). This is a genuine scope question the words do not settle. It does not unseat the verdict, because the same Spirit-and-knowing cluster recurs in 1 Corinthians 2:10 to 16, 1 John 2:27, and Ephesians 1:17 to 18, all addressed to general readerships, carrying the illumination of believers regardless of how the maximal apostolic reading of this single verse resolves.

The phrases the natural person does not receive (psychikos anthropos ou dechetai) and is not able to know (ou dynatai gnonai) could be read to deny any natural cognitive grasp of the text at all, which would prove too much, since unbelievers plainly can parse the words on a page. The verb is spiritually examined (anakrinetai) is in the ongoing passive form, and the verbs receive (dechomai) and know (ginosko) here concern reception and salvific apprehension, the spiritual discernment of verse 15, not bare literacy. So the verse marks the faculty needed for spiritual apprehension, which is exactly the Spirit-given understanding the proposition asserts.

The revelatory weight of he will announce the things coming (anangelei ta erchomena) and the unveiling vocabulary reveal (apokalypto) and revelation (apokalypsis) raises a second scope question, whether illumination conveys genuinely new content or grants understanding of the already given word. The lexicon carries both senses. Ephesians 1:18 enlighten (photizo) and Luke 24:45 open the mind (dianoigo) plus Psalm 119:18 open (gal, from galah, uncover) point to understanding of existing content, while reveal (apokalypto) and announce (anangello) can denote fresh disclosure. The words do not rank these, so the verdict affirms the core claim while leaving this content-versus-understanding scope underdetermined, which is why divergence among readers is lexically explicable.

variant_units_examined.note: The conjunction at the head of verse 10, de (but or and) versus gar (for) across manuscript witnesses, does not touch the revelatory verb revealed (apekalypsen) or its agent God through the Spirit (ho theos dia tou pneumatos). Not in the ingested ECM apparatus window (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants), assessed from word-form analysis only.

Whether the from-form (genitive, the 'from-X' grammatical form) reads Spirit (pneumatos) or Holy Spirit (hagiou pneumatos) in taught by the Spirit (didaktois pneumatos) is a stylistic expansion. The Spirit-taught-words clause and its sense are stable. Not in ECM scope (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants).

The simple statement of fact form you remain (menete) versus the command reading and the it remains (menei) variant of remain (meno) affect mood, not the didactic action of the anointing (chrisma), which is the verb teaches (didaskei). Not in ECM scope (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants).

variants.note: No cited verse falls in the ingested ECM apparatus window (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants), which is 3 John 1:1 to 1:15, so variants here are assessed from word-form analysis and known apparatus signals rather than CBGM (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method used in modern critical editions). The examined units are stylistic and do not unseat the lexical pattern.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The perception and teaching verbs, reveal (apokalypto, a completed past action in the active voice), search (eraunao, ongoing simple statement of fact), teach (didasko), guide (hodegeo, future), enlighten (photizo, completed action whose result still stands, passive), and open the mind (dianoigo, completed past action), place the action with God or the Spirit and the believer as recipient in the dative case (the 'to-X' form) and accusative case (the direct-object form) pronouns. The natural-person versus spiritual-person (psychikos versus pneumatikos) contrast in 1 Corinthians 2:14 to 15 grammatically forecloses the natural faculty, so the text affirms Spirit-given spiritual understanding.

The Old Testament pattern of the Spirit (ruach) of wisdom and understanding in Isaiah 11:2 and the petition to have the eyes opened to the torah (the law of Moses) in Psalm 119:18 carry forward into the Helper's (Parakletos) teaching office in John 14 and 16 and the apostolic letters, showing one covenantal arc in which the Spirit leads God's people into the truth of the word.

On the reading that the Spirit's office is to grant understanding of the already given word rather than to add new content, Ephesians 1:18 enlightens the eyes to know what is declared, Luke 24:45 opens the mind to understand the existing Scriptures, and Psalm 119:18 asks for sight of wonders already in the torah (the law of Moses). This lens affirms the proposition directly and reads it as illumination of Scripture in the strict sense.

On the reading that the cluster is primarily revelatory, the words reveal (apokalypto) and revelation (apokalypsis) in 1 Corinthians 2:10 and Ephesians 1:17 and he will announce the things coming (anangelei ta erchomena) in John 16:13 denote fresh disclosure rather than mere comprehension of prior text. This lens still affirms the proposition, since the Spirit is the agent giving believers understanding of God's truth, but it reads the scope as broader than the written word alone.

Read strongly, John 16:13 he will guide you into all the truth (hodegesei hymas eis ten aletheian pasan) is a promise to the apostolic circle that grounds the foundational deposit of truth, with the announcing of coming things as a special office. On this lens the verse itself is bounded, yet the proposition still stands for all believers because 1 Corinthians 2, 1 John 2:27, and Ephesians 1:17 to 18 address general readerships and supply the believer-wide illumination.

hermeneutics.notes: There is no lexical conflict over whether the Spirit gives understanding, every lens affirms that. The genuine divergence among readers is over scope, content versus understanding and apostolic versus all-believer, and the vocabulary underdetermines both. The flag progressive_revelation is marked true because the verdict traces an Old Testament to New Testament arc from the Spirit (ruach) of wisdom and the opened eyes upon the torah (the law of Moses) to the Helper (Parakletos) and the apostolic letters.

stem_audit.notes: The stem uses illumine, Spirit, Scripture, and spiritual understanding, which are biblical and descriptive vocabulary. The claim does not encode a tradition-specific taxonomy or smuggle its own conclusion, so the verdict is derived from the lexical data on the original stem. The cross-references cited in the prior evidence file were labeled source tsk (Treasury of Scripture Knowledge) but the actual store relationship for those exact verse pairs is OPENBIBLE_CROSS_REF from OpenBible-cross-refs, so the source label and vote counts have been corrected to openbible against queried data. This is a data-integrity fix and does not change the verdict.

lay_summary: Across the cited passages the words used for what God and the Spirit do line up cleanly with the proposition, and the grammar makes the picture firm. In 1 Corinthians 2:10 God revealed (apekalypsen, a completed past action) these things through the Spirit, who searches (eraunai, an ongoing simple statement) even the deep things of God. Verse 12 says believers received the Spirit so that they may know the things freely given, and verse 13 says the words are taught by the Spirit (didaktois pneumatos). Verse 14 says the natural person is not able to know them because they are spiritually examined (anakrinetai, a form where the action is done to them), and verse 16 says believers have the mind of Christ (noun Christou). John 16:13 says the Spirit will guide (hodegesei, a future action) into all the truth, John 14:26 that the Helper (Parakletos) will teach all things, Ephesians 1:18 that the eyes of the heart are enlightened (pephotismenous, a completed action whose result still stands) to know what is already declared, and Luke 24:45 that Christ opened the mind (noun) to understand the Scriptures. Psalm 119:18 asks God to open (gal, from the Hebrew verb galah, meaning uncover) the eyes to see wonders in his written law (torah). The agent is always God or the Spirit, the recipient is the believer, and the object is the truth of God including the written word, and the pattern runs from the Old Testament psalm and prophecy through the gospels into the letters, so the confidence is high. Where careful readers diverge is only about scope, and that divergence comes from the words themselves. Some terms, like reveal (apokalypto) and announce the coming things (anangello), can mean brand new content, while others, like enlighten (photizo) the eyes and open the mind (dianoigo) to understand the Scriptures, clearly mean grasping what is already given, and the vocabulary does not rank which is primary. Likewise the promise to guide into all the truth is spoken to a small group, so the words leave open whether all the truth is everything or the apostolic deposit. None of these open questions reverses the core claim that the Spirit gives believers spiritual understanding of God's word.
